Five teams that benefit most from 3-on-3 overtime--Article Inside

I'll copy and paste any ESPN Insider articles I find..

It’s gotten a bit lost in the wave of news that surrounds the NHL draft and free agency. Even with all the impact moves that have been made, one decision by the NHL GMs that could have a bigger impact on the standings than any trade or signing is the decision to immediately go to 3-on-3 in overtime.

To placate the players’ concern over extending overtime, there won’t be 4-on-4 next season in overtime and it has the potential to not only wipe out of the shootout, but to give teams that excel in 3-on-3 a decided advantage in a tight playoff race.

Last year in the AHL where the seven-minute overtime was split in half by 4-on-4 and 3-on-3, 201 of the 268 overtime games were decided before the shootout. That was 75 percent, up from 35.3 percent the previous season. With the exclusive use of 3-on-3, the NHL projects to be even higher. It’s not a stretch to suggest that a good 80 percent of the overtime games will end before the shootout.

“Oh, no doubt. It’s going to end fast,” said John Torchetti, head coach of the AHL’s Iowa Wild. “The skill level comes out. I think the fans are going to really enjoy it. I enjoyed coaching it.”

Over the course of the season, Torchetti and his colleagues in the AHL learned several things about the 3-on-3 OT.

Typically, teams played two forwards and one defensemen. Some experimented with three forwards but defensive mistakes are magnified significantly, often turning into a series of odd-man rushes.

So ideally, teams will have a defenseman strong at leading the transition but also sound defensively.

The other thing that Torchetti said becomes absolutely critical is winning faceoffs.

“The match-up is right away. You can’t just try to cheat and get a puck,” he said. “It’s about having a better idea of where they’re going to go and the coverages, the guys behind you. The first guy is the centerman, the defenseman goes behind for a one-timer off the draw and you have to have good angles off that. You have to notice more if guys are on the forehand or backhand coming off cycles.”

Match-ups are also magnified, so the home team has a definite advantage according to Torchetti. He also agreed that teams with goalies who play the puck well will have an advantage in jump-starting the offensive attack.

There’s going to be a ton of double-shifting in overtime and Torchetti said a typical rotation looks like this: first unit, second unit, first unit, second unit, third unit, first unit, second unit, first unit, second unit.

With all that in mind, here’s a look at the five teams that will take most advantage of the new overtime role and dominate the 3-on-3 play. 1. Chicago Blackhawks

2014-15 shootout record: 9-3

This rule doesn’t necessarily benefit the Blackhawks in the standings because they were already good in the shootout thanks to Jonathan Toews and Patrick Kane, who each had six shootout goals last season. But a first 3-on-3 unit consisting of Toews, Kane and Duncan Keith is hard to top. It fulfills all of the requirement you want from a 3-on-3 unit. Toews consistently wins faceoffs, at a rate of 56.5 percent last season. Keith can skate like the wind and will be able to get back to defend and lead the transition.

And as good as Kane was in the shootout, it’ll be even more fun to see what he can do on the open ice with teammates.

“He’s going to have some new moves,” Torchetti said.

The fascinating thing to watch will be whether or not Joel Quenneville trusts his youth in overtime, as he has a second unit featuring Teuvo Teravainen and Artemi Panarin that would be fun to watch. 2. Pittsburgh Penguins

Shootout record: 4-6

This is another dream team when it comes to 3-on-3. There is a little concern in the faceoff circle where both Sidney Crosby and Evgeni Malkin were below 50 percent last year but we’re splitting hairs. A trio of Crosby, Phil Kessel and Kris Letang would be ridiculous. If Mike Johnston decides to split the centers up he has Kessel, David Perron and Patric Hornqvist at his disposal on the wing.

Had this been implemented last season, the Penguins aren’t playing in ten shootouts. It’s fair to project another four points to their total which would have put them second in the Metropolitan, where they would have avoided the Rangers in round one. 3. Tampa Bay Lightning

Shootout record: 3-5

The Lightning is a team that has historically struggled in the shootout despite the individual offensive talent that has gone through the franchise. The transition to 3-on-3 will be a good one for Tampa, a team that would have won the Atlantic last year with a little better success in the shootout.

Victor Hedman and his huge strides is another ideal defenseman anchor for 3-on-3 and he showed off a play-making ability during the playoffs that he didn’t have earlier in his career. Steven Stamkos will be hard to stop with that much ice.

The question becomes whether or not coach Jon Cooper splits up the triplets in 3-on-3. Here’s hoping that Cooper at least gives that trio a crack at playing together in overtime as the rare three-forward group. Ondrej Palat is responsible defensively and the sixth sense in which these three play will be magnified in overtime. 4. Los Angeles Kings

Shootout record: 2-8

The Kings are on this list because of Drew Doughty and the impact removing the shootout will have on their team. Again, if this was implemented last season, the Kings probably make the playoffs and then anything happens. Who would have felt comfortable picking the Ducks over the Kings in round one last spring?

Doughty will get leaned on heavily in overtime. Anze Kopitar is strong on faceoffs and has more offensive flair than his two-way game allows him to show off during 5-on-5. Jeff Carter and Tyler Toffoli headline the second unit, although there’s a significant drop on defense when Doughty leaves the ice, assuming he ever does.

The Dallas Stars are another team to consider in this spot, with a top unit of Tyler Seguin, Jamie Benn and John Klingberg that is loaded with firepower. 5. Detroit Red Wings

Shootout record: 4-10

The Red Wings are another team that has struggled in the shootout over the course of the last few seasons and it was their GM Ken Holland who led the campaign to minimize the shootout.

Now, with the addition of defenseman Mike Green, the Red Wings will be exceedingly dangerous in overtime and they have a coach in Jeff Blashill who is one of the few in the league with experience coaching 3-on-3 from his time in Grand Rapids.

The ideal split of talent in Detroit would be a top unit of Pavel Datsyuk, Tomas Tatar and Mike Green. When Datsyuk and Tatar played together last season at even strength, they controlled 60.4 percent of the shot attempts. Put them with Green and it’ll be fun to watch. That would leave a second unit of Henrik Zetterberg, Gustav Nyquist and Niklas Kronwall, not flashy but a solid group that should be better than most second units.

Let’s say Detroit wins half the shootout games it lost last season, putting them at 105 points -- no longer a playoff bubble team, but instead a team pushing for an Atlantic division title. That’s exactly the kind of impact this rule change could end up having on the standings.

They won't be nearly as top-tier as the five in the article, but in terms of how good the previous vs new overtimes are for the team, The Avalanche are gonna benefit a good deal.

TIL To send Ctrl+Alt+Del over Windows RDP you have to use Ctrl+Alt+End
Well Bill Gates wanted one button for that function, but IBM had to go and get all awkward about it!
That's actually pretty interesting. TIL worthy even....

For a control input that was chosen to have such a drastic consequence, IBM's choice was the smarter. Imagine accidental reboots because you bumped that single key, or the keyswitch was mechanically failing. Separate guards in the form of a multi-key sequence is sound engineering just as multiple, concurring key turns were required to launch Titan nuclear missiles.

Microsoft's insistence on making things easy and convenient for stupid people just to increase market share without thinking through the potential consequences (or caring about them) is damned near criminal. Remember the AutoRun days for untrusted media and executable e-mail attachments? It's no different than manufacturing guns without safetys just so "Grandma doesn't get confused by another button." I'd love to see a class action lawsuit for damages caused by negligent defaults and stupid decisions in the name of convenience.
